case_info.explanation: Retained PFO in the vitreous and subretinal space after retinal surgery B. Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation. Fundus photographs revealed PFO bubbles in the inferior retina (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.

Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation.
